sections.title: What are 1D Arrays?
sections.content:
**Arrays** are the most fundamental data structure in programming. Every other structure - stacks, queues, heaps, hash tables - is built on top of arrays or inspired by their properties. Mastering arrays is not a prerequisite for DSA; it *is* DSA at its foundation.

An array stores elements in **contiguous memory locations**. Because of this, accessing any element by index is O(1) - the CPU can jump directly to `base_address + index * element_size`. This is the defining property of arrays and the reason they're used everywhere. The tradeoff: inserting or deleting at the middle requires shifting elements - O(n) cost.

**Cache locality** is why arrays are fast in practice beyond their asymptotic complexity. Modern CPUs load memory in cache lines (blocks of ~64 bytes). When you access `arr[i]`, the CPU also preloads `arr[i+1]`, `arr[i+2]`, etc. Sequential array traversal therefore benefits from hardware prefetching. Linked lists, which scatter nodes in memory, lose this advantage entirely.

In JavaScript, arrays are dynamic - they resize automatically. Under the hood, V8 uses actual contiguous memory when all elements are the same type (called a 'fast array'). Once you mix types or create sparse arrays, V8 falls back to a hash-map representation that loses the cache advantage. This is worth knowing when writing performance-sensitive code.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Arrays are the default data structure - you'll use them in almost every problem. The specific techniques in this topic have more precise triggers. Prefix sums are the right tool whenever a problem asks about sums over a range or subarray. The write-pointer (in-place) technique appears when the problem says 'O(1) extra space' or 'modify the array in place'. Kadane's algorithm applies to any 'maximum sum contiguous subarray' formulation.
signals: sum of elements in a subarray or range
range sum queries on a static array
find the subarray with a given property

sections.explanation: Three essential array templates: prefix sum with 1-indexed prefix array for clean range queries, Kadane's for maximum subarray via running optimal state, and write pointer for in-place filtering without extra space.

items.name: Circular Arrays
items.description: Some problems treat the array as circular - index `n` wraps around to `0`. Use `index % n` for all accesses. For maximum subarray in a circular array, the answer is either the standard Kadane's result or `totalSum - minSubarraySum` (the subarray not included wraps around the ends).

items.name: Sorted Arrays
items.description: A sorted array enables binary search (O(log n) lookup), two-pointer techniques for pair problems, and prefix sum with binary search for count queries. Many problems give a sorted constraint specifically to enable these efficient approaches.
items.example_problem: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

items.name: Difference Arrays
items.description: The inverse of prefix sums: to apply a range update `[l, r] += val` in O(1), modify a difference array at positions l and r+1, then reconstruct the array with a prefix sum. Enables O(1) range updates and O(n) final reconstruction.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n) for single traversal, O(1) per prefix sum query after O(n) build
sections.space: O(n) for prefix sum array, O(1) for in-place traversal algorithms
sections.explanation: A single pass over the array is the baseline O(n) cost - you must visit each element at least once to consider it. Prefix sums trade O(n) space for converting O(n) per query into O(1), a classic space-time tradeoff. In-place techniques (write pointer, reversal) achieve O(n) time with O(1) space by using the input array itself for output.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mutating an array while iterating over it: deleting or inserting elements during a for loop changes indices mid-iteration, causing elements to be skipped or processed twice. Use a write pointer or collect results in a separate pass.
JavaScript's `arr.sort()` is lexicographic by default: `[1, 10, 2].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 2]` not `[1, 2, 10]`. Always pass a comparator: `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)` for ascending numeric sort.

Copying arrays with `=` copies the reference, not the values: `const copy = original` makes both variables point to the same array. Modifying `copy` modifies `original`. Use `const copy = [...original]` or `original.slice()` for a shallow copy.

Forgetting the empty array edge case: `arr[0]` on an empty array is `undefined`, not an error, which silently corrupts Kadane's algorithm and other single-element initializations. Check `if (!arr.length) return` or equivalent before entering.

Off-by-one in prefix sum range queries: for a 1-indexed prefix array, the range sum `[l, r]` (0-indexed) is `pre[r+1] - pre[l]`, not `pre[r] - pre[l-1]`. Mixing these indexing conventions is a constant source of wrong answers.

items.title: Two Sum
items.why: Tests the fundamental array traversal with a hash map complement lookup - the most common array problem pattern.

items.title: Maximum Subarray
items.why: Direct application of Kadane's algorithm - tests understanding of maintaining optimal running state during traversal.

items.title: Product of Array Except Self
items.why: Requires prefix product and suffix product arrays - direct extension of prefix sum technique to multiplicative context.

items.title: Container With Most Water
items.why: Tests two-index traversal from both ends with a clear invariant - the pointer that moves is always the shorter wall.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: A matrix is an array of arrays - the traversal patterns, prefix sums, and in-place techniques you just learned extend directly to two dimensions, with the added challenge of spatial reasoning about rows, columns, and diagonals.
